title: Sherlock Holmes and the Red-Headed League
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
retoldBy: Retold for Grammar Stream from “The Red-Headed League” by Arthur Conan Doyle (1891)
blurb: Cases for Young Detectives. Why would anyone pay a red-haired shopkeeper four pounds a week to copy out an encyclopedia? Sherlock Holmes studies the knees of a young man’s trousers and uncovers a secret tunnel heading for a cellar full of gold.
note: A retelling for young readers that keeps Doyle’s plot, clues and deductions. Changes: Holmes’s pipe, the whisky and Watson’s revolver are left out; John Clay reaches for a tool rather than a pistol, and is not called a murderer; the remark about who pierced Spaulding’s ears is dropped. Short explanations (a pawnbroker, the Encyclopaedia Britannica) and “Clue check” questions are added.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Man with Fiery Hair
paragraphs: One autumn morning I called on my friend Mr Sherlock Holmes at his rooms in Baker Street. I found him talking to a stout, red-faced old gentleman with the most astonishing hair I had ever seen. It was not ginger, and it was not orange. It was a bright, blazing red, like a bonfire.
“You could not have come at a better time, my dear Watson,” said Holmes. “This is Mr Jabez Wilson. Mr Wilson, this is Dr Watson, who has helped me in many of my cases.”
The stout gentleman gave me a nod, pulled a crumpled newspaper from his coat pocket and began searching through it.

While he searched, I studied him. Holmes is always telling me to *observe*, so I tried my best to notice clues, the way he does. But I could see nothing special: baggy checked trousers, a rather dirty black coat, a brassy watch-chain, and that blazing red head.
Holmes saw what I was doing and smiled.

“Apart from the obvious facts,” he said, “that Mr Wilson has done hard work with his hands, that he belongs to the Freemasons, that he has been to China, and that he has done a great deal of writing lately, I can deduce nothing else.”
Mr Wilson nearly jumped out of his chair. “How in the world did you know all that, Mr Holmes? It is true! I started out as a ship’s carpenter.”

“Your right hand is quite a size larger than your left,” said Holmes. “You have worked hard with it, and the muscles have grown. You are wearing the Freemasons’ badge, that little pin shaped like an arc and a compass. Your right cuff is very shiny, and your left sleeve has a smooth, worn patch near the elbow, where you rest it on a desk to write. And the fish tattooed above your wrist has its scales coloured a delicate pink, which is done only in China. There is a Chinese coin on your watch-chain, too.”
Mr Wilson laughed loudly. “Well, I never! I thought at first you had done something clever, but I see there was nothing in it after all.”
“I begin to think, Watson,” sighed Holmes, “that I make a mistake in explaining. Now, Mr Wilson, have you found the advertisement?”
“Here it is,” said Mr Wilson. “This is what started it all.”
I took the newspaper and read aloud:

“TO THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE. There is a vacancy for a member of the League. The pay is four pounds a week, for very easy work. All red-headed men who are healthy and over twenty-one may apply. Apply in person on Monday, at eleven o’clock, to Mr Duncan Ross, 7 Pope’s Court, Fleet Street.”
“What on earth does it mean?” I said.
Holmes chuckled and wriggled in his chair, which is what he does when he is very pleased. “It is a little out of the ordinary, isn’t it? Now, Mr Wilson, tell us everything.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Red-Headed League
paragraphs: “I own a small pawnbroker’s shop in Saxe-Coburg Square,” Mr Wilson began. (A pawnbroker lends people money. They leave something valuable with him, such as a watch, and when they pay the money back they get the watch back. Pawnbrokers’ shops have three golden balls hanging over the door.)

“I have one assistant, a young man called Vincent Spaulding. He works for half the usual wages, because he wants to learn the business. His only fault is that he loves photography. He is always diving down into the cellar like a rabbit into its hole, to develop his pictures.”
“I see,” said Holmes, and his eyes gleamed.

“Eight weeks ago, Spaulding showed me this advertisement. ‘I wish I had red hair, Mr Wilson,’ he said. ‘The League was started by a rich American with red hair. When he died, he left his money to pay red-headed men for easy jobs. But only real, bright, blazing red will do. Hair like yours!’

“So we shut the shop and went to Fleet Street. Oh, Mr Holmes! Every man in London with a touch of red in his hair was there: straw, lemon, orange, brick, every shade you can think of. The street looked like a barrow full of oranges. Spaulding pushed and squeezed me through the crowd and into the office.

“Behind a table sat a little man with hair even redder than mine. He found something wrong with every other man and sent him away. But when he saw me, he leapt up and said he had never seen hair so fine. Then he grabbed it with both hands and tugged until I yelled. ‘There are tears in your eyes,’ he said. ‘All is as it should be. We have been fooled twice by wigs and once by paint.’ And he leaned out of the window and told the crowd the place was filled.

“Mr Duncan Ross, for that was his name, told me my work. I must sit in that office every morning from ten o’clock until two. I must never leave the room, not even for a moment, or I would lose the job forever. And I must copy out the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* by hand.”
The *Encyclopaedia Britannica* is a huge set of books, with facts about everything in the world, from A to Z. Copying it out would take years.

“I thought it must be a joke,” said Mr Wilson. “But the next morning I bought some ink and paper and went. Mr Ross started me on the letter A, and every Saturday he paid me four golden sovereigns. Week after week I wrote about Abbots and Archery and Armour and Architecture, and I never once dared to leave the room.
“Then, this morning, the door was locked. There was a little card nailed to it. Here it is.”
On the card was written: THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED.
Holmes and I looked at the card, and then at Mr Wilson’s cross face, and we could not help it. We both burst out laughing.
“I cannot see what is so funny!” cried Mr Wilson, turning as red as his hair.
“No, no,” said Holmes, pushing him gently back into his chair. “I would not miss your case for the world. What did you do next?”

“The landlord had never heard of the League. He said the red-headed man had moved out yesterday, and gave me a new address. But it was a factory that made artificial kneecaps, and nobody there had heard of him. Spaulding said I should just wait for a letter. But I don’t want to lose such a good job, Mr Holmes. So I came to you.”
“You were quite right to come,” said Holmes. “I think this may be more serious than it looks.”
Clue check: Somebody paid Mr Wilson a lot of money just to stay away from his shop every morning. Why might somebody want him out of the way?

chapters.title: Chapter 3. The Knees of His Trousers
paragraphs: Before Mr Wilson left, Holmes asked him about his assistant.
“Spaulding came to work for you three months ago, and it was he who showed you the advertisement? What does he look like?”
“Small and quick, with no beard, though he must be nearly thirty. He has a white splash on his forehead, where some acid burned him once.”
Holmes sat up very straight. “I thought as much,” he said. “Are his ears pierced for earrings?”
“Why, yes, sir!”
“Thank you, Mr Wilson. Today is Saturday. I hope that by Monday I shall have an answer for you.”
When Mr Wilson had gone, Holmes curled up in his armchair with his knees under his chin and his eyes shut. “Please do not speak to me for fifty minutes, Watson,” he said.
I was nearly asleep myself when he sprang up. “Put on your hat,” he said. “We are going to Saxe-Coburg Square.”

It was a shabby little square of dingy brick houses around a patch of weedy grass. On one corner hung three golden balls and a sign saying JABEZ WILSON. Holmes walked slowly up the street and back again, looking closely at the houses. Then, to my surprise, he banged the pavement hard with his walking stick, two or three times, right in front of the shop. At last he knocked on the door.
A bright-looking, clean-shaven young man opened it.
“Excuse me,” said Holmes. “How would I get to the Strand?”
“Third on the right, fourth on the left,” said the young man quickly, and shut the door.
“Smart fellow, that,” said Holmes as we walked away. “I should say he is the fourth smartest man in London.”
“You only asked the way so that you could see him,” I said.
“Not him, Watson. The knees of his trousers.”
“And what did you see?”
“What I expected to see.”
“And why did you bang on the pavement?”
“My dear Doctor, this is a time for looking, not for talking. We are spies in an enemy’s country. Let us see what lies behind the square.”

Round the corner, what a difference! Behind the sleepy square ran one of the busiest streets in London, full of carriages and grand shops. Holmes read out the names of the buildings, one by one, to fix them in his memory: the tobacconist’s, the newspaper shop, the Coburg branch of the City and Suburban Bank, a restaurant, and a carriage-builder’s.
“And now our work is done,” he said. “Let us go and hear some violin music.”
All afternoon Holmes sat in the concert hall, smiling dreamily and waving his long fingers in time to the music. Afterwards, he turned to me.

“This business is serious, Watson,” he said. “A big crime is about to happen, and I believe we shall be just in time to stop it. Come to Baker Street at ten o’clock tonight, and wear your warmest coat. We may have a long wait in the dark.”
Then he vanished into the crowd. I went home puzzling. I had seen everything Holmes had seen, yet he seemed to know what was going to happen, and I had no idea at all.
Clue check: Holmes wanted to see the knees of Spaulding’s trousers. What sort of work makes trousers dirty and worn at the knees? And what building was right behind Mr Wilson’s shop?

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Waiting in the Dark
paragraphs: At ten o’clock that night, Holmes had two visitors: Mr Jones, a detective from Scotland Yard, and a long, thin, gloomy gentleman called Mr Merryweather.
“I hope this is not a wild goose chase,” said Mr Merryweather. “It is the first Saturday night for twenty-seven years that I have missed my game of cards.”
“You will find tonight’s game more exciting,” said Holmes. “And for you, Jones, there is the man you most want to catch.”

“John Clay!” said Jones. “The cleverest thief in London, Dr Watson. His grandfather was a duke, and his brain is as quick as his fingers. I have been on his trail for years and never even seen his face.”

Two cabs carried us back to the busy street behind Saxe-Coburg Square. Mr Merryweather unlocked a side door, then an iron gate, then another. We went down a winding stone staircase and along a dark passage that smelt of earth, into a huge cellar piled high with wooden crates.
Mr Merryweather tapped his stick on the stone floor. “Why, dear me! It sounds hollow!”
“Please be quiet!” said Holmes sharply. “You may have spoiled everything. Kindly sit on that box and touch nothing.”
Holmes knelt on the floor with his lantern and his magnifying glass and studied the cracks between the stones. Then he jumped up, looking satisfied.

“We have an hour,” he said. “They will wait until Mr Wilson is asleep. Watson, this is the cellar of the City and Suburban Bank. Mr Merryweather is in charge of the bank, and he will tell you why thieves are so interested in it.”
“It is our French gold,” whispered Mr Merryweather. “Thirty thousand gold coins, borrowed from the Bank of France. The box I am sitting on holds two thousand of them.”
I stared at the crates all around us. There was a fortune in that cellar!
“Now we must hide in the dark,” said Holmes. “When I flash my light on them, close in quickly. Jones, have you done what I asked?”
“Three policemen are waiting at the front door of Mr Wilson’s shop.”
“Then every hole is stopped. Silence!”

Holmes slid the shutter across his lantern, and we were plunged into the blackest darkness I have ever known. I crouched behind a crate in the cold, damp air, hardly daring to breathe. It was only an hour and a quarter, but it felt like the whole night.
Then, suddenly, I saw a glint of light.

At first it was a tiny spark on the stone floor. Then it grew into a yellow line. And then, without a sound, a crack seemed to open in the floor, and out of it came a hand, a white, slim hand, feeling about in the little patch of light.
Clue check: Now can you guess why Spaulding spent so much time in the cellar, and why his trousers were worn at the knees?

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Tunnel
paragraphs: With a scraping, grinding sound, one of the big floor-stones tipped over, leaving a square black hole. Lantern-light streamed out. Over the edge peeped a clean-cut, boyish face. The young man pulled himself up and out, and then helped up a second man, with a pale face and a mop of very red hair.
“It’s all clear,” whispered the first man. “Have you got the chisel and the bags? Great Scott! Jump, Archie, jump!”

For Sherlock Holmes had sprung out and seized him by the collar. The red-headed man dived back down the hole. Jones grabbed at his coat-tails, but he wriggled free and was gone. The first man reached for something in his pocket, but Holmes brought his hunting crop down on his wrist, and a heavy tool clattered on to the stones.
“It is no use, John Clay,” said Holmes calmly. “You have no chance at all.”
“So I see,” said the young man, as cool as you please. “My friend has got away, though.”
“There are three policemen waiting for him at the door.”
“Oh, indeed! You seem to have thought of everything. I must congratulate you.”
“And I you,” said Holmes. “Your red-headed idea was very clever.”
Jones snapped a pair of handcuffs on the prisoner’s wrists.
“Kindly do not touch me with your hands,” said John Clay grandly. “I have royal blood in my veins. And when you speak to me, always say ‘sir’ and ‘please’.”
Jones grinned. “All right,” he said. “Would you *please*, *sir*, march upstairs, where we can get a cab to carry your Highness to the police station?”
“That is better,” said John Clay. He made a sweeping bow to the three of us and walked quietly away with the detective.
Very early the next morning, back in Baker Street, Holmes explained everything.

“It was clear from the start that the Red-Headed League was only a way of getting Mr Wilson out of his shop for a few hours every day. Four pounds a week was nothing to the thieves, for they were hoping to win thousands. One rented the office, and the other made sure Mr Wilson applied for the job.

“When I heard the assistant worked for half wages, I knew he had some strong reason for wanting that job. Then I remembered his habit of vanishing into the cellar. The cellar! Something was being done down there, for hours every day, for weeks. What could it be? I could think of only one thing. He was digging a tunnel to another building.

“So we went to the square. I banged on the pavement to find out whether the cellar stretched out in front of the shop. It did not, so the tunnel must go another way. When the assistant opened the door, I looked at his knees. You must have noticed how worn and stained they were, from hours of digging. Then I walked round the corner and saw that the bank was right behind Mr Wilson’s shop. The puzzle was solved.”
“And how did you know they would come tonight?” I asked.

“When they closed the League office, they no longer needed Mr Wilson out of the way. So the tunnel was finished. They had to use it soon, before it was found or the gold was moved. And Saturday was best, because the bank is closed on Sunday, which gave them two whole days to escape.”
“You reasoned it out beautifully,” I said. “It is such a long chain, and yet every link holds.”
Holmes yawned and stretched out his long legs. “It saved me from being bored,” he said. “These little problems help me to escape from the ordinary, dull days.”

As for Mr Jabez Wilson, he never did get to the letter B. But he kept the thirty-two pounds he had earned, and he knew more about Abbots and Archery and Armour than anybody else in Saxe-Coburg Square.
